extracted.intended_audience: federal judges preparing jury instructions, patent litigators, and jurors in U.S. patent trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for use in United States district court patent trials, explaining legal standards the jury must apply for issues such as claim construction, infringement, invalidity, and damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: What a patent is and how one is obtained
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains that a United States patent is granted by the PTO, gives the patent owner the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, offering to sell, or importing the patented invention in the U.S., and that the patent application includes a specification and claims defining the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes prosecution, the role of the PTO examiner, prior art searching, office actions, prosecution history, and notes that a PTO grant does not conclusively establish validity because the court can find claims invalid based on evidence not considered by the PTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent at issue (identification of claims and parties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies the asserted patent and claims, the parties (patent holder and alleged infringer), the accused products/methods, and what the jury must decide (infringement, invalidity, and damages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Template instructions for presenting the patent, specification, drawings and claims to jury; reminds jury that willfulness (if at issue) is a separate finding that should not affect damage award directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction / interpretation of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge interprets the meaning of claim language; claims are numbered sentences that set forth requirements (elements/limitations) that define the boundaries of the patent's protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must accept the court's definitions of claim terms and apply those definitions to issues of infringement and invalidity; coordinate with special instructions for means-plus-function claims. Authorities cited: Markman, Phillips, Pitney Bowes, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overview of applicable law — claim-by-claim assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is assessed on a claim-by-claim basis; there may be infringement as to one claim but not another. There are different ways a patent may be infringed (direct, contributory, inducement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may give preliminary overview to focus jury on relevant facts; will provide detailed instructions later. Invalidity may be shown for reasons such as lack of novelty or obviousness; written description and enablement defenses also explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Two standards of proof apply: the preponderance of the evidence standard (more likely than not) and the higher clear and convincing evidence standard (highly probable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement is proved by a preponderance of the evidence; invalidity must be shown by clear and convincing evidence. Distinguishes these civil standards from the criminal 'beyond a reasonable doubt' standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement — general rule and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holder must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the requirements for one or more types of infringement (direct, inducement, contributory) are met for an asserted claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces the specific instructions for literal infringement, doctrine of equivalents, inducement, contributory infringement, and willfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct literal infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove literal infringement, the patent holder must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the accused product or process meets all of the requirements of a claim (each and every element) and was made/used/sold/imported without permission during the patent term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accused product/method does not have every requirement of the claim, there is no literal infringement. Addresses treatment of dependent claims (dependent claims incorporate all requirements of the claim they reference) and notes that knowledge of the patent or infringement is irrelevant to literal infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement under the doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the accused product/method does not literally meet every claim requirement, it can infringe under the doctrine of equivalents if it includes parts/steps identical or equivalent to the claim requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalency is judged by whether differences were insubstantial as of the time of alleged infringement or whether the accused part performed substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result (function-way-result test). Known interchangeability as of the time of alleged infringement may be considered. The patentee must prove equivalency by a preponderance of the evidence. Doctrine cannot be used to capture what was already in the prior art or to cover subject matter described but not claimed in the patent. Burden-shifting: alleged infringer first produces evidence that the accused matter is in the prior art, then patentee must show it is not in the prior art or would not have been obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claims — literal infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function claim limitations cover only the specific structure disclosed in the specification for performing the claimed function and the equivalents of those specific structures, not all possible structures that could perform the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will identify the corresponding structure in the specification for each means-plus-function limitation. Jury must determine (1) whether the accused product has structure performing the claimed function, and (2) whether that structure is the same as or equivalent to the disclosed structure. Equivalence judged by insubstantial differences or function-way-result as of the time the patent issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement by combined acts of multiple parties
rubrics_metrics.description: When no single party performs all steps of a claimed method but multiple parties together perform every step, the claim is directly infringed only if all steps are performed by or attributable to a single entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An entity is responsible for others' performance when it directs or controls others' performance or when the actors form a joint enterprise. A joint enterprise requires proof of four elements: agreement, common purpose, community of pecuniary interest, and equal right to control/direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement involving system components outside the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: When some system components are located outside the U.S., direct infringement requires that the accused system include every element of the claim and that control of the system was exercised and the benefit of the system was enjoyed in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent holder must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that control and beneficial use occurred in the U.S. Authorities cited (NTP, Akamai, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may be liable for contributory infringement for offering to sell or selling an item that is an important component of the invention, so that the buyer directly infringes the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be a contributory infringer one must know that the part is especially made or adapted for use in an infringement, and the component must not be a staple or common component suitable for substantial non-infringing uses. For damages, patentee must prove either the accused product necessarily infringes or prove acts of direct infringement by others to which the accused contributor made a substantial contribution; damages limited by number of direct acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducing (active) infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Induced infringement requires proof that the accused infringer took actions that knowingly and intentionally induced another to commit acts that constitute direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To recover damages for induced infringement, patentee must prove the accused product necessarily infringes or prove acts of direct infringement by others that were induced. Damages are limited by the number of instances of direct infringement (must prove number of direct acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement (finding separate from damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: If willfulness is at issue, the jury must make a finding as to whether any infringement was willful; that finding should not directly affect the damages award, though the court may take willfulness into account later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction separates the willfulness finding from the calculation of damages; further legal guidance on enhanced damages and factors may be provided by the court (not fully reproduced here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — general grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be invalid for a number of reasons including lack of novelty (anticipation), obviousness, failure to meet the written description requirement, and failure to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidity is a defense to infringement; the alleged infringer must prove invalidity by clear and convincing evidence. The instructions explain specific doctrines (anticipation, obviousness, written description, enablement, statutory bars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The party asserting invalidity must prove by clear and convincing evidence that a claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court will instruct the jury on what 'clear and convincing' means; invalidity issues (e.g., anticipation, obviousness) are analyzed claim-by-claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet the written description requirement, the patent's specification must be detailed enough to demonstrate that the applicant actually possessed the invention as broadly as claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification does not show possession of the claimed subject matter, the claim may be invalid for lack of written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet the enablement requirement, the patent's description must be sufficiently full and clear to have allowed persons of ordinary skill in the field to make and use the invention without undue experimentation at the time the patent application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of enablement is a ground for invalidity; instructions discuss the undue experimentation standard and timing (as of the filing date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art — definition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art generally includes things that existed before the claimed invention and were publicly known, used, or described in publications or patents anywhere; prior art is used to assess novelty and obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court to instruct jury on what constitutes prior art for the case; examiner's cited references are listed on the patent but the jury may consider other prior art presented at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated (not new) if all of the elements of the claim are present in a single previous device or method or are sufficiently described in a single previous printed publication or patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires that a single prior art reference disclose every claim element; the alleged infringer must prove anticipation by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be barred under statutory provisions (e.g., on-sale or public disclosure before critical dates) that prevent patenting of subject matter disclosed or publicly used prior to the patent application's critical date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court will apply relevant statutory bar doctrines (e.g., on-sale bar) as applicable to the case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — Graham framework and secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be invalid as obvious even if no single prior art reference discloses every claim element; the jury must consider (1) scope and content of the prior art, (2) differences between the prior art and the claimed invention, (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art, and (4) objective evidence of non-obviousness (secondary considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instruction lays out these sub-questions and directs the jury to weigh evidence such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, copying, and other objective indicia. The alleged infringer must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct inventorship is required; claims may be invalid if inventorship is incorrect or if persons who should be named as inventors are omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventorship issues can affect validity and ownership; the jury may be instructed on relevant proof needed for inventorship disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If the jury finds infringement of a claim that is not invalid, it must determine money damages to compensate the patent holder for the infringement; damages should put the patent holder in approximately the same financial position it would have been in had the infringement not occurred and must be at least a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages are compensatory, not punitive; jury may not award fines or penalties beyond compensation. The court will provide detailed instructions for lost profits, reasonable royalties, and other damage considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent holder bears the burden of proving damages and the amount by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury should consider the evidence presented to calculate damages (lost profits, reasonable royalty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — entitlement and Panduit-type factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profits are recoverable when the patent holder demonstrates by a preponderance of the evidence that it would have made additional sales 'but for' the infringement; typical test elements include demand for the patented product, absence of acceptable noninfringing alternatives, the patent holder's capacity to exploit the demand, and the amount of profit that would have been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instructions expand these into related considerations such as market share, collateral sales, price erosion, and other economic evidence; jury may consider expert testimony and other business evidence. The court provides subsections on Lost Profits – Factors to Consider, Market Share, Collateral Sales, Price Erosion, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — entitlement, definition, and Georgia-Pacific factors
rubrics_metrics.description: If lost profits cannot be proven, the patent holder is entitled at minimum to a reasonable royalty — the payment that would have resulted from a hypothetical negotiation between the patent holder and infringer at the time infringement began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instruction lists the Georgia-Pacific factors (15 factors) to guide the reasonable royalty calculation, including (1) royalty rates on comparable licenses, (2) rates paid by the patent holder, (3) the nature and scope of the license, (4) the licensor's established policy, (5) commercial relationship of the parties, (6) profitability and advantages of the patented invention, (7) existing noninfringing alternatives, (8) duration and term of the license, (9) established profitability of the product, (10) utility and advantages of the patent over old modes, (11) extent of use of the invention and established profitability, (12) customary portion of profit or selling price allowing for use of the invention, (13) portion of profits credited to the invention versus other factors, (14) opinion and testimony of experts, and (15) the hypothetical negotiation consideration (what a prudent licensee and patentee would have agreed to). It emphasizes no single factor is dispositive and the jury may consider other relevant factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of commencement of damages and marking/notice rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages for products begin on the date the alleged infringer both infringed and was notified of the patent, unless the patent holder marked the product; marking (placing 'patent' or 'pat.' and patent number on products or public web notice) can start damages without actual notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent holder has the burden to prove substantial compliance with marking. If not marked, damages begin upon actual notice (e.g., date of complaint) or earlier if patentee proves earlier actual notice. Special rule: method (process) claims have no notice requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 287(c)(2)(F); damages for method claims begin on the earlier of patent issuance or date infringement began.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculating damages for inducement or contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover damages for induced or contributory infringement, patentee must prove that the accused product necessarily infringes or must prove acts of direct infringement by others that were induced or substantially contributed to, and must prove the number of direct acts because damages are limited by the number of direct infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages may be shown by individual acts of direct infringement or by showing a class of products/uses that directly infringe; authorities include Dynacore and Cardiac Pacemakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glossary / definitions control
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical terms and legal terms used in the instructions have definitions which must be followed and control the jury's deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides definitions of terms such as abstract, amendment, anticipation, claim, conception, continuations, elements, enablement, infringement, limitation, nonobviousness, office action, prior art, prosecution history, reads on, reduction to practice, reexamination, requirement, royalty, specification, etc., to ensure jurors understand specialized vocabulary used in instructions.
